explanations.equipment-safety__OFF-2018-Q30: With fresh gas flowing, the inspiratory unidirectional valve is held shut during expiration, so continuing fresh gas cannot go forwards - it can only reach the compliant reservoir bag by travelling BACKWARDS along the rail and down through the absorbent. That makes the bag mount (E), the bag-to-absorber conduit (B), the canister and the absorber-to-fresh-gas rail (C) all bidirectional over the respiratory cycle, and the patient limb beyond the Y-piece (A) is bidirectional in every circumstance. The stub between the fresh gas inlet and the inspiratory valve (D) is the one segment bounded by the gas source upstream and a closed one-way valve downstream, so gas there only ever moves towards the patient. Precondition worth noting: at zero fresh gas flow the retrograde limb disappears and this distinction breaks down.
explanations.equipment-safety__18A-59: The common limb between the Y-piece and the patient carries inspired gas out and expired gas back through the same lumen, so it is bidirectional unconditionally - at any fresh gas flow and in any ventilation mode. The inspiratory and expiratory limbs are each guarded by a one-way valve, and gas leaving the APL valve goes only to scavenging. Caveat: option D is a defensible second answer, because with fresh gas flowing the soda lime does carry retrograde flow towards the reservoir bag during expiration (this is what the companion question 18B-116 tests); A remains the single best answer because it holds without any such precondition.
explanations.cardiovascular__18B-54:
Phentolamine blocks α-adrenoceptors, producing arterial and venous dilation. Reduced resistance to venous return increases the slope of the vascular (venous return) function curve - the curve plotted here, venous return against right atrial pressure - so it rotates or tilts upward. Venodilation may slightly reduce mean systemic filling pressure, moving the x-intercept a little to the left, but the predominant graphical effect is the upward rotation caused by the reduced resistance to venous return.

Source: Guyton & Hall Physiology, p. 252; Pappano & Wier (2018), Ch 10
